source.title: Benign Overfitting in Two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Yuan Cao; Zixiang Chen; Misha Belkin; Quanquan Gu

record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically studies benign and harmful overfitting in a synthetic two-patch data model using two-layer CNNs; it does not test random-label fitting or the other listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper's results concern learning a signal or memorizing label-independent noise in its synthetic data model, not fitting a completely random relabeling of training images. These results are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited random-label findings from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes fitting clean, signal-bearing labels using either a shared signal patch or an independent noise patch. Its random binary labels determine the signal patch y·µ, so they are not random relabelings independent of the inputs. Neither its loss bounds nor its signal/noise dynamics test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Under the stated assumptions, the authors establish signal learning with small training and population loss in one SNR regime, and noise memorization with small training but constant-order population loss in the opposite regime.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical gradient-descent analysis of a two-layer CNN on a synthetic signal-plus-noise distribution, rather than empirical fitting of randomly relabeled image datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on the signal-to-noise ratio regime: n·SNR^q = Ω̃(1) yields small test loss, while n⁻¹·SNR⁻q = Ω̃(1) yields constant-order test loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Condition 4.2 and n·SNR^q = Ω̃(1), gradient descent reaches training loss ≤ ε and population loss ≤ 6ε + exp(−n²), learning the signal while noise coefficients remain small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A two-layer CNN can achieve small training and population loss on this synthetic signal-plus-noise distribution in the high-SNR regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Condition 4.2 and n⁻¹·SNR⁻q = Ω̃(1), gradient descent reaches training loss ≤ ε with Θ(1) population loss, memorizing noise patches without sufficiently learning the signal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A two-layer CNN can fit this synthetic training distribution through noise-patch memorization while retaining constant-order population loss in the low-SNR regime.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and limited to a specific synthetic data distribution and two-layer CNN architecture; it does not empirically test random labels or real image datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported results directly bear on the listed claim versions. Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 each provide one training-loss and one test-loss result, all included.

untested.parts: Completely random relabeling, near-zero training error and chance test error, with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or wholly Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across a label-corruption sweep.
Effects of weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning real-label patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels. The paper instead compares signal-patch learning with noise-patch memorization under clean labels.

record.verdict_notes: The phase boundary is characterized up to logarithmic factors; Figure 1 leaves an intermediate band uncharacterized. Suggested label-flip extensions are not analyzed results. The row states indicate inability to assess the listed versions, not failure of the stated theorems.

versions.untested_parts: Randomly relabeled training images; chance test error; unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels, and convergence as corrupted-label fraction changes.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from clean to fully corrupted labels and the corresponding test-error curve.
Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and their effects on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, including the claimed comparison over training.
